claim: The vertebrate retina consists of ~100 cell types in total.
source: It consists of ~100 cell types in total (Shekhar et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2020), including ~30 types of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) that send the retinal output signals to the brain via the optic nerve (Sanes and Masland, 2015; Baden et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Shekhar et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2020).

claim: The vertebrate retina includes ~30 types of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs).
source: It consists of ~100 cell types in total (Shekhar et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2020), including ~30 types of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) that send the retinal output signals to the brain via the optic nerve (Sanes and Masland, 2015; Baden et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Sanes and Masland, 2015; Baden et al., 2016).

claim: RGCs send retinal output signals to the brain via the optic nerve.
source: It consists of ~100 cell types in total (Shekhar et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2020), including ~30 types of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) that send the retinal output signals to the brain via the optic nerve (Sanes and Masland, 2015; Baden et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Sanes and Masland, 2015; Baden et al., 2016) and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Each RGC type forms distinct neural circuits within the retina to extract specific features of the visual image such as color, contrast, and motion.
source: Each of these RGC types forms distinct neural circuits within the retina to extract specific features of the visual image coming into the eye, such as color, contrast, and motion.
evidence: The claim represents established scientific knowledge about retinal function.

claim: The retina performs parallel and dynamic processing as the first stage of the visual pathway.
source: The retina thus performs parallel and dynamic processing as the first stage of the visual pathway.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about retinal function.

claim: Most knowledge on retinal function has been obtained from ex vivo studies.
source: Most of our knowledge on retinal function has been obtained from ex vivo studies because isolated retinal tissues are nevertheless functional, for example, responsive to light (Barlow et al., 1964).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation (Barlow et al., 1964) and represents a general statement about the field.

claim: Isolated retinal tissues are functional and responsive to light.
source: Most of our knowledge on retinal function has been obtained from ex vivo studies because isolated retinal tissues are nevertheless functional, for example, responsive to light (Barlow et al., 1964).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Barlow et al., 1964).

claim: Ex vivo physiological approaches cannot perform long-term recordings.
source: First, one cannot perform long-term recordings (Meister et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Meister et al., 1994).

claim: Ex vivo approaches cannot avoid artifacts due to retinal dissection, such as the effect of cutting RGC axons.
source: Second, one cannot avoid artifacts due to retinal dissection, such as the effect of cutting RGC axons (Vidal-Sanz et al., 2017) or retinal epithelial detachment (Strauss, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Vidal-Sanz et al., 2017; Strauss, 2005).

claim: Neuromodulatory effects of retinopetal pathways are difficult to study in an isolated retinal preparation.
source: Neuromodulatory effects of retinopetal pathways are also difficult to study in an isolated retinal preparation (Repérant et al., 2006; Esposti et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Repérant et al., 2006; Esposti et al., 2013).

claim: In vivo studies are indispensable for understanding to what degrees knowledge on the retina can be translated from ex vivo to fully physiological in vivo conditions.
source: In vivo studies are thus indispensable for understanding to what degrees our knowledge on the retina can be translated from ex vivo to fully physiological in vivo conditions and clarifying retinal function thoroughly.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the limitations of ex vivo studies.

claim: Previous physiological studies on the retina in vivo were conducted mostly under anesthetized and often paralyzed conditions.
source: Previous physiological studies on the retina in vivo were conducted mostly under anesthetized—and often paralyzed—conditions.
evidence: The claim represents a general statement about the field's historical practices.

claim: Single-unit recordings were made directly from the retina to monitor RGC activity in vivo.
source: To monitor RGC activity in vivo, for example, single-unit recordings were made directly from the retina (Kuffler, 1953), at the optic nerve or tract fibers (Hartline, 1938; Lettvin et al., 1959; Enroth-Cugell and Robson, 1966; Mastronarde, 1983; Mastronarde, 1985; Sagdullaev and McCall, 2005), or in the form of 'slow-potential' in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN; Bishop et al., 1962; Kaplan and Shapley, 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Kuffler, 1953).

claim: Only a handful of studies have reported awake recordings from the retina or its outputs.
source: In contrast, thus far only a handful of studies have reported awake recordings from the retina (Esposti et al., 2013; Hong et al., 2018) or its outputs (Weyand, 2007; Liang et al., 2018; Liang et al., 2020; Schröder et al., 2020; Sibille et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research and represents a statement about the state of the field.

claim: It remains unclear what exactly the eye tells the brain in awake animals.
source: Thus, despite a long history of research on the retina, it still remains unclear what exactly the eye tells the brain in awake animals.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the limited number of awake studies.

claim: Systematic studies on the early visual pathway showed higher firing activity in both dLGN and the superior colliculus of awake animals than those under anesthesia.
source: For example, systematic studies on the early visual pathway showed higher firing activity and faster response dynamics in both dLGN (Durand et al., 2016) and the superior colliculus (SC; De Franceschi and Solomon, 2018) of awake animals than those under anesthesia.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Durand et al., 2016; De Franceschi and Solomon, 2018).

claim: Systematic studies on the early visual pathway showed faster response dynamics in both dLGN and the superior colliculus of awake animals than those under anesthesia.
source: For example, systematic studies on the early visual pathway showed higher firing activity and faster response dynamics in both dLGN (Durand et al., 2016) and the superior colliculus (SC; De Franceschi and Solomon, 2018) of awake animals than those under anesthesia.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Durand et al., 2016; De Franceschi and Solomon, 2018).

claim: The optic tract is a bundle of nerve fibers composed of RGC axons as they project from the eye to their main targets: dLGN and SC.
source: Specifically, the electrodes were placed in the optic tract (OT), a bundle of nerve fibers composed of RGC axons as they project from the eye to their main targets: dLGN and SC (Ellis et al., 2016; Román Rosón et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Ellis et al., 2016; Román Rosón et al., 2019).

claim: OT recordings are superior to direct in vivo retinal recordings because the retinal circuits and the eye optics remain intact.
source: These recordings are superior to direct in vivo retinal recordings (e.g., with epiretinally implanted mesh electrodes; Hong et al., 2018) because the retinal circuits and the eye optics remain intact, and also to those extracellular recordings in SC (Sibille et al., 2022) or dLGN (Weyand, 2007) because RGC axonal signals do not need to be disambiguated from those of local axons or somata.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the advantages of the recording method.

claim: OT recordings are superior to extracellular recordings in SC or dLGN because RGC axonal signals do not need to be disambiguated from those of local axons or somata.
source: These recordings are superior to direct in vivo retinal recordings (e.g., with epiretinally implanted mesh electrodes; Hong et al., 2018) because the retinal circuits and the eye optics remain intact, and also to those extracellular recordings in SC (Sibille et al., 2022) or dLGN (Weyand, 2007) because RGC axonal signals do not need to be disambiguated from those of local axons or somata.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about the advantages of the recording method.

claim: The study made 17 chronic recordings (75 cells) and 80 acute recordings (207 cells without anesthesia; 325 cells with isoflurane; 103 cells with FMM).
source: In total, we made 17 chronic (75 cells) and 80 acute recordings (207 cells without anesthesia; 325 cells with isoflurane; 103 cells with FMM), where a standardized set of visual stimuli were presented to the subject animal to characterize the visual response properties of the recorded cells (for ~1 hr; Figure 1A, B; see Methods for details).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Isolated units typically had a triphasic spike waveform as expected from axonal signals.
source: Isolated units typically had a triphasic spike waveform (e.g., Figure 1F–H) as expected from axonal signals (Barry, 2015) and most of them had a minimum interspike interval above 2 ms (e.g., Figure 1I–K; 93%, awake; 94%, isoflurane; 99%, FMM).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (Figure 1F-H) and a citation (Barry, 2015).

claim: Most isolated units had a minimum interspike interval above 2 ms (93%, awake; 94%, isoflurane; 99%, FMM).
source: Isolated units typically had a triphasic spike waveform (e.g., Figure 1F–H) as expected from axonal signals (Barry, 2015) and most of them had a minimum interspike interval above 2 ms (e.g., Figure 1I–K; 93%, awake; 94%, isoflurane; 99%, FMM).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data (Figure 1I-K) from the study.

claim: In both anesthetized and awake conditions, around 20–50% of cells were ON cells, 10–40% were ON/OFF cells, and 20% were OFF cells.
source: In both anesthetized and awake conditions, we found around 20–50% of ON cells, 10–40% of ON/OFF cells, and 20% of OFF cells in our data sets.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: About half of the cells (42–54%) were either OS or DS or both in the anesthetized conditions regardless of their response polarities or anesthetics.
source: In the anesthetized conditions, about a half of the cells (42–54%) were either OS or DS or both regardless of their response polarities or anesthetics.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The fraction of DS/OS cells in anesthetized conditions is consistent with a previous in vivo study but rather higher than one would expect from anatomical and physiological studies ex vivo.
source: This is consistent with a previous in vivo study (Hong et al., 2018), but rather higher than one would expect from anatomical and physiological studies ex vivo (about a third; Sanes and Masland, 2015; Baden et al., 2016; Jouty et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Hong et al., 2018; Sanes and Masland, 2015; Baden et al., 2016; Jouty et al., 2018).

claim: Much less DS/OS cells (17%) were found in the awake condition.
source: In contrast, we found much less DS/OS cells (17%) in the awake condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The discrepancy in the fraction of DS/OS cells between awake and anesthetized conditions likely arose from a difference in the baseline firing rate.
source: This discrepancy in the fraction of DS/OS cells cannot be explained by a sampling bias per se, if any, because we used the same experimental setup between the anesthetized and awake recordings. Instead, it likely arose from a difference in the baseline firing rate (see below and Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and the definition of DS/OS index.

claim: Higher firing in the awake condition generally leads to a larger denominator in the DS/OS index calculation, hence a lower DS/OS index value.
source: Since DS/OS index is defined as a normalized population vector (Equation 3 in Methods; Mazurek et al., 2014), higher firing in the awake condition generally leads to a larger denominator, hence a lower DS/OS index value.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the mathematical definition of the DS/OS index.

claim: Baseline firing rates were significantly higher in awake mice (20 ± 27 Hz; median ± interquartile range) than in those under anesthesia (isoflurane, 2 ± 6 Hz, p < 0.001; FMM, 2 ± 4 Hz, p < 0.001).
source: First, we found significantly higher baseline firing rates in awake mice (B = 20 ± 27 Hz; median ± interquartile range) than in those under anesthesia (isoflurane, 2 ± 6 Hz, p < 0.001, U-test; FMM, 2 ± 4 Hz, p < 0.001; Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 3D) with statistical analysis.

claim: Awake ON cells had particularly high baseline activity (up to ~100 Hz).
source: Awake ON cells had particularly high baseline activity (up to ~100 Hz) and showed a prominent reduction in firing rates in response to light decrements (see Figure 3B for example).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 3B).

claim: Many awake ON cells showed virtually no responses to light increments (N = 36 out of 84), except for a sharp rebound response to a full-contrast inversion (N = 26 out of 36).
source: In contrast, due to this high baseline activity, many of them showed virtually no responses to light increments (N = 36 out of 84), except for a sharp rebound response to a full-contrast inversion (N = 26 out of 36; see Figures 2A and 3B for example).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figures 2A and 3B).

claim: OFF-suppressive ON cells primarily encode light decrements by decreasing firing from their high baseline firing rates (62 ± 32 Hz, mean ± standard deviation).
source: This indicates that they primarily encode light decrements by decreasing firing from their high baseline firing rates (62 ± 32 Hz, mean ± standard deviation), rather than light increments by increasing firing as conventional ON cells do (Masland, 2012; Sanes and Masland, 2015; Baden et al., 2016; Jouty et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study and citations to published research.

claim: OFF-suppressive responses were barely observed in anesthetized animals (isoflurane, 2/325 cells; FMM, 1/103 cells).
source: Indeed, such responses were barely observed in anesthetized animals (isoflurane, 2/325 cells; FMM, 1/103 cells; Figure 2H1) where the baseline firing rate was generally low (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 2H1, Figure 3D).

claim: The awake responses had a larger dynamic range than those under anesthesia.
source: Second, we found that the awake responses had a larger dynamic range than those under anesthesia.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The absolute amplitude of the evoked responses from the baseline was larger for the awake condition (|A| = 45 ± 55 Hz) than for anesthetized conditions (isoflurane, 30 ± 31 Hz, p < 0.001; FMM, 27 ± 33 Hz; p < 0.001).
source: Specifically, the absolute amplitude of the evoked responses from the baseline was larger for the awake condition (Figure 3E; awake, |A| = 45 ± 55 Hz, median ± interquartile range; isoflurane, 30 ± 31 Hz, p < 0.001, Mann–Whitney U-test against awake data; FMM, 27 ± 33 Hz; p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 3E) with statistical analysis.

claim: At low stimulus contrast, a higher sensitivity was found in the awake condition (estimated evoked response at 10% contrast = 7 ± 13 Hz) than under anesthesia (isoflurane, 4 ± 12 Hz, p < 0.001; FMM, 3 ± 10 Hz, p < 0.001).
source: At low stimulus contrast, we found a higher sensitivity in the awake condition (estimated evoked response at 10% contrast = 7 ± 13 Hz, median ± interquartile range) than under anesthesia (isoflurane, 4 ± 12 Hz, p < 0.001, Mann–Whitney U-test; FMM, 3 ± 10 Hz, p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: The maximum sensitivity to a change in contrast was comparable between the awake and anesthetized conditions (|Aλ/4| = 5 ± 11 Hz/%contrast; isoflurane, 6 ± 9 Hz/%contrast; FMM, 5 ± 7 Hz/%contrast; p = 0.1).
source: However, the maximum sensitivity to a change in contrast—that is, the slope size at the midpoint of the sigmoid—was comparable between the awake and anesthetized conditions (|Aλ/4| = 5 ± 11 Hz/%contrast; isoflurane, 6 ± 9 Hz/%contrast; FMM, 5 ± 7 Hz/%contrast; p = 0.1, Kruskal–Wallis test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: A significant phase shift in the responses was found between the recording conditions.
source: We also found a significant phase shift in the responses between the recording conditions (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 3F).

claim: The phase was on average smallest for the awake condition (−1.9 ± 0.6 and 1.7 ± 0.6 radian) compared to isoflurane (−0.9 ± 0.6 and 2.0 ± 0.5 radian; p < 0.001 for both cases) and largest for the FMM anesthesia (−0.5 ± 0.8 and 2.3 ± 0.5 radian).
source: In both clusters, we found that the phase was on average smallest for the awake condition (−1.9 ± 0.6 and 1.7 ± 0.6 radian, respectively; mean ± standard deviation; isoflurane, −0.9 ± 0.6 and 2.0 ± 0.5 radian; p < 0.001 for both cases, t-test), while largest for the FMM anesthesia (−0.5 ± 0.8 and 2.3 ± 0.5 radian; p = 0.007 and p = 0.044 against corresponding isoflurane data, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: The response dynamics are faster in awake mice than those under anesthesia, especially with FMM.
source: This implies that the response dynamics are faster in awake mice than those under anesthesia, especially with FMM.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the phase shift data.

claim: In awake mice, most cells responded faithfully to all the stimulation frequencies tested from 1.875 to 15 Hz.
source: In awake mice, most cells responded faithfully to all the stimulation frequencies we tested from 1.875 to 15 Hz (see Figure 4A for example).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 4A).

claim: Some awake cells showed the largest responses to the 15 Hz stimulation, suggesting that they were possibly tuned to even higher frequencies.
source: Some awake cells showed the largest responses to the 15 Hz stimulation (Figure 4A; curve fit quality with Equation 4), suggesting that they were possibly tuned to even higher frequencies.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figure 4A).

claim: In the anesthetized conditions, retinal output responses typically followed the stimulation frequencies up to 7.5 Hz, but failed to do so at 15 Hz.
source: In the anesthetized conditions, in contrast, retinal output responses typically followed the stimulation frequencies up to 7.5 Hz, but failed to do so at 15 Hz (see Figure 4B for example).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 4B).

claim: In the awake condition, a larger number of cells responded well at medium frequencies (3.75 Hz, 63%; 7.5 Hz, 71%) than at a low frequency (1.875 Hz, 59%).
source: In the awake condition, a larger number of cells responded well at medium frequencies (3.75 Hz, 63%; 7.5 Hz, 71%) than at a low frequency (1.875 Hz, 59%); and the majority of the awake cells remained responsive to a high-frequency stimulus (15 Hz, 47%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The majority of the awake cells remained responsive to a high-frequency stimulus (15 Hz, 47%).
source: In the awake condition, a larger number of cells responded well at medium frequencies (3.75 Hz, 63%; 7.5 Hz, 71%) than at a low frequency (1.875 Hz, 59%); and the majority of the awake cells remained responsive to a high-frequency stimulus (15 Hz, 47%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Under anesthesia, the fraction of responsive cells was the largest at a low frequency (1.875 Hz; isoflurane, 77%; FMM, 67%).
source: Under anesthesia, in contrast, the fraction of responsive cells was the largest at a low frequency (1.875 Hz; isoflurane, 77%; FMM, 67%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Only a small fraction of the anesthetized cells were able to follow the stimulation frequency at 15 Hz (isoflurane, 13%; FMM, 3%).
source: Fewer cells responded robustly at faster flicker rates (3.75 and 7.5 Hz; isoflurane, 69% and 67%, respectively; FMM, 63% and 59%), and only a small fraction of the anesthetized cells were able to follow the stimulation frequency at 15 Hz (isoflurane, 13%; FMM, 3%).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The retinal output dynamics are faster in awake animals than those under anesthesia, especially for FMM.
source: Consistent with the analysis of the response phase (Figure 3), these outcomes indicate that the retinal output dynamics are faster in awake animals than those under anesthesia, especially for FMM.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on temporal frequency responses.

claim: The ex vivo data lied in-between awake and anesthetized conditions in terms of response kinetics.
source: Interestingly, we identified that the ex vivo data lied in-between.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The ex vivo STAs had significantly longer peak latencies (64 ± 28 ms, p < 0.001) and lower peak frequencies (4.3 ± 1.8 Hz, p < 0.001) than the awake ones.
source: The ex vivo STAs had significantly longer peak latencies (64 ± 28 ms, p < 0.001) and lower peak frequencies (4.3 ± 1.8 Hz, p < 0.001) than the awake ones.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: The peak latencies were significantly shorter in an isolated retinal preparation than in the anesthetized conditions (isoflurane, p < 0.001; FMM, p < 0.001).
source: In contrast, the peak latencies were significantly shorter in an isolated retinal preparation than in the anesthetized conditions (isoflurane, p < 0.001; FMM, p < 0.001), while the peak frequencies were comparable between these conditions (isoflurane, p = 0.3; FMM, p = 0.052).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: Awake responses are faster and their kinetics are more similar across different cell classes than ex vivo or anesthetized responses.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that awake responses are faster and their kinetics are more similar across different cell classes than ex vivo or anesthetized responses.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on temporal filters.

claim: The mean firing rate during the white-noise stimulus presentation was significantly higher in awake (34.9 ± 24.6 Hz) than in all the other recording conditions (isoflurane, 13.0 ± 13.1 Hz; FMM, 10.9 ± 10.7 Hz; ex vivo, 6.9 ± 6.6 Hz; all with p < 0.001).
source: The mean firing rate during the white-noise stimulus presentation was significantly higher in awake (34.9 ± 24.6 Hz; mean ± standard deviation) than in all the other recording conditions (isoflurane, 13.0 ± 13.1 Hz; FMM, 10.9 ± 10.7 Hz; ex vivo, 6.9 ± 6.6 Hz; all with p < 0.001, t-test in the logarithmic scale; Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 6A) with statistical analysis.

claim: The maximum projected light intensity was comparable between in vivo (~31 mW/m2 at the eye) and ex vivo setups (~36 mW/m2 on the isolated retina).
source: The maximum projected light intensity was comparable between in vivo (~31 mW/m2 at the eye; see Methods) and ex vivo setups (~36 mW/m2 on the isolated retina; Vlasiuk and Asari, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study and a citation (Vlasiuk and Asari, 2021).

claim: Due to absorption by the eye optics, photon flux at the retina was estimated to be ~10 times lower for in vivo than for ex vivo recordings (on the order of 103 and 104 R*/photoreceptor/s, respectively).
source: Due to absorption by the eye optics, however, photon flux at the retina was estimated to be ~10 times lower for in vivo than for ex vivo recordings (on the order of 103 and 104 R*/photoreceptor/s, respectively; see Methods).
evidence: The claim is based on calculations from experimental data and known optical properties.

claim: The neutral firing rate was significantly higher in the awake condition (29.3 ± 22.5 Hz) than those under anesthesia (isoflurane, 9.5 ± 11.9 Hz, p < 0.001; FMM, 7.5 ± 9.3 Hz, p < 0.001).
source: Consistent with the results on the baseline firing rates measured by the sinusoidally flickering stimuli (Figure 3), the neutral firing rate was significantly higher in the awake condition (29.3 ± 22.5 Hz, mean ± standard deviation) than those under anesthesia (isoflurane, 9.5 ± 11.9 Hz, p < 0.001, t-test on a log scale; FMM, 7.5 ± 9.3 Hz, p < 0.001; Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 6C) with statistical analysis.

claim: The neutral firing rates ex vivo (5.5 ± 7.1 Hz) were as low as those in the anesthetized conditions (isoflurane, p = 0.02; FMM, p = 0.1), and significantly lower than those in the awake condition (p < 0.001).
source: We also found that the neutral firing rates ex vivo (5.5 ± 7.1 Hz) were as low as those in the anesthetized conditions (isoflurane, p = 0.02; FMM, p = 0.1), and significantly lower than those in the awake condition (p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: The midpoint of the sigmoid fitted to ex vivo responses (1.6 ± 1.4) was significantly higher than that for in vivo responses (isoflurane, 1.1 ± 0.9; FMM, 1.1 ± 0.8; awake, 0.8 ± 1.0; all with p < 0.001).
source: Second, the midpoint of the sigmoid fitted to ex vivo responses (1.6 ± 1.4, median ± interquartile range) was significantly higher than that for in vivo responses (isoflurane, 1.1 ± 0.9; FMM, 1.1 ± 0.8; awake, 0.8 ± 1.0; all with p < 0.001, Mann–Whitney U-test; Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 6H) with statistical analysis.

claim: In vivo responses are more linearized to cover a larger dynamic range, especially in the awake condition due to high neutral responses.
source: In agreement with the outcomes obtained with the sinusoidally flickering stimulus (Figure 3), this suggests that in vivo responses are more linearized to cover a larger dynamic range, especially in the awake condition due to high neutral responses (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figure 6G).

claim: The dynamic range was generally largest in the awake condition (56 ± 54 Hz) and significantly larger for in vivo (isoflurane, 26 ± 30 Hz; FMM, 29 ± 27 Hz) than for ex vivo (12 ± 12 Hz, all with p < 0.001).
source: Indeed, while certain batch effects existed across recording sessions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), the dynamic range computed from the gain function (see Methods) was generally largest in the awake condition (56 ± 54 Hz; median ± interquartile range) and significantly larger for in vivo (isoflurane, 26 ± 30 Hz; FMM, 29 ± 27 Hz) than for ex vivo (12 ± 12 Hz, all with p < 0.001, Mann–Whitney U-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) with statistical analysis.

claim: In vivo responses had a slightly but significantly higher information rate in bits per second (isoflurane, 8.6 ± 5.9 bits/s; FMM, 7.6 ± 3.6 bits/s; awake, 7.5 ± 2.2 bits/s) than ex vivo responses (6.2 ± 1.9 bits/s; p < 0.001, p = 0.004, p < 0.001, respectively).
source: Overall, we found that in vivo responses had a slightly but significantly higher information rate in bits per second (Figure 7A; isoflurane, 8.6 ± 5.9 bits/s; FMM, 7.6 ± 3.6 bits/s; awake, 7.5 ± 2.2 bits/s; median ± interquartile range) than ex vivo responses (6.2 ± 1.9 bits/s; p < 0.001, p = 0.004, p < 0.001, respectively; Mann–Whitney U-test), but a lower information rate in bits per spike (Figure 7B; isoflurane, 1.2 ± 1.6 bits/spike; FMM, 1.3 ± 1.4 bits/spike; and awake, 0.3 ± 0.3 bits/spike; against ex vivo, 2.3 ± 1.9 bits/spike; all with p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 7A) with statistical analysis.

claim: In vivo responses had a lower information rate in bits per spike (isoflurane, 1.2 ± 1.6 bits/spike; FMM, 1.3 ± 1.4 bits/spike; and awake, 0.3 ± 0.3 bits/spike) than ex vivo responses (2.3 ± 1.9 bits/spike; all with p < 0.001).
source: Overall, we found that in vivo responses had a slightly but significantly higher information rate in bits per second (Figure 7A; isoflurane, 8.6 ± 5.9 bits/s; FMM, 7.6 ± 3.6 bits/s; awake, 7.5 ± 2.2 bits/s; median ± interquartile range) than ex vivo responses (6.2 ± 1.9 bits/s; p < 0.001, p = 0.004, p < 0.001, respectively; Mann–Whitney U-test), but a lower information rate in bits per spike (Figure 7B; isoflurane, 1.2 ± 1.6 bits/spike; FMM, 1.3 ± 1.4 bits/spike; and awake, 0.3 ± 0.3 bits/spike; against ex vivo, 2.3 ± 1.9 bits/spike; all with p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 7B) with statistical analysis.

claim: The amount of information conveyed by a single spike in awake cells was the lowest due to high average firing rates (34 ± 25 Hz).
source: In particular, the amount of information conveyed by a single spike in awake cells was the lowest due to high average firing rates (34 ± 25 Hz; mean ± standard deviation).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on information rates and firing rates.

claim: The retinal coding in vivo is less efficient than that ex vivo.
source: This indicates that the retinal coding in vivo is less efficient than that ex vivo (Schwartz, 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the information theoretic analysis and supported by a citation (Schwartz, 2021).

claim: The information estimated with the rate code was significantly larger for simulated awake responses (3.4 ± 1.2 bits) than for anesthetized (isoflurane, 3.0 ± 0.8 bit, p <0 .001; FMM, 3.0 ± 0.8 bit, p = 0.011) or ex vivo responses (2.4 ± 1.3 bit, p < 0.001).
source: We found that the information estimated with the rate code was significantly larger for simulated awake responses (3.4 ± 1.2 bits; median ± interquartile range) than for anesthetized (isoflurane, 3.0 ± 0.8 bit, p <0 .001, Mann–Whitney U-test; FMM, 3.0 ± 0.8 bit, p = 0.011) or ex vivo responses (2.4 ± 1.3 bit, p < 0.001; Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling analysis based on experimental data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Information in the latency-based temporal code of the simulated awake responses (1.9 ± 1.1 bits) was comparable to that of ex vivo responses (1.7 ± 1.3 bits, p = 0.6), but significantly lower than those calculated from the simulated anesthetized responses (isoflurane, 2.3 ± 0.6 bits; FMM, 2.4 ± 0.6 bits; both with p < 0.001).
source: In contrast, information in the latency-based temporal code of the simulated awake responses (1.9 ± 1.1 bits) was comparable to that of ex vivo responses (1.7 ± 1.3 bits, p = 0.6), but significantly lower than those calculated from the simulated anesthetized responses (isoflurane, 2.3 ± 0.6 bits; FMM, 2.4 ± 0.6 bits; both with p < 0.001; Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling analysis based on experimental data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).

claim: The rate code is in favor of awake responses, while the temporal code is not.
source: Thus, our results suggest that the rate code is in favor of awake responses, while the temporal code is not.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the modeling analysis.

claim: Single-cell linear decoding performance was comparable across recording conditions (awake, R = 0.20 ± 0.13; isoflurane, 0.24 ± 0.04; FMM, 0.24 ± 0.06; ex vivo, 0.20 ± 0.10).
source: We found that single-cell linear decoding performance was comparable across recording conditions (awake, R = 0.20 ± 0.13, curve fit parameter a with 95% confidence interval; isoflurane, 0.24 ± 0.04; FMM, 0.24 ± 0.06; ex vivo, 0.20 ± 0.10).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling analysis based on experimental data.

claim: At the population level, Pearson's R reached 0.6 in about a third of the cases in the awake recordings with less than 10 cells to be considered, but none in the anesthetized recordings with less than 20 cells; and at least ~30 cells were required for the ex vivo recordings.
source: At the population level, however, Pearson's R reached 0.6 in about a third of the cases in the awake recordings with less than 10 cells to be considered, but none in the anesthetized recordings with less than 20 cells; and at least ~30 cells were required for the ex vivo recordings (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling analysis based on experimental data (Figure 8).

claim: The exponential saturation constant was smaller for the awake responses (b = 8 ± 4) than for the anesthetized (isoflurane, 23 ± 7; FMM, 21 ± 6) or ex vivo responses (72 ± 36).
source: Consistent with this observation, the exponential saturation constant was smaller for the awake responses (b = 8 ± 4 from Equation 10; an estimate with 95% confidence interval) than for the anesthetized (isoflurane, 23 ± 7; FMM, 21 ± 6) or ex vivo responses (72 ± 36).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling analysis based on experimental data.

claim: Retinal population responses in awake mice are more linearly decodable than in the other recording conditions.
source: This indicates that retinal population responses in awake mice are more linearly decodable than in the other recording conditions, even though an image reconstruction is not necessarily the objective function of the retina.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the linear decoding analysis.

claim: Awake response properties were overall similar to those under isoflurane or FMM anesthesia or ex vivo.
source: We found that awake response properties were overall similar to those under isoflurane or FMM anesthesia (2—4) or ex vivo (Figures 5 and 6); however, we identified three distinct features in the awake condition besides behavioral effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Schröder et al., 2020): higher firing rates, a larger dynamic range (Figures 3 and 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and faster response dynamics (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figures 2-6).

claim: Three distinct features were identified in the awake condition: higher firing rates, a larger dynamic range, and faster response dynamics.
source: We found that awake response properties were overall similar to those under isoflurane or FMM anesthesia (2—4) or ex vivo (Figures 5 and 6); however, we identified three distinct features in the awake condition besides behavioral effects (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Schröder et al., 2020): higher firing rates, a larger dynamic range (Figures 3 and 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and faster response dynamics (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figures 3-6).

claim: The awake response properties made the awake responses less efficient from an information theoretic viewpoint but more linearly decodable at the population level.
source: These properties made the awake responses less efficient from an information theoretic viewpoint (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) but more linearly decodable at the population level (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling analysis based on experimental data (Figures 7-8).

claim: Knowledge on retinal physiology cannot be simply translated from ex vivo to in vivo conditions.
source: Our results highlight that our knowledge on retinal physiology cannot be simply translated from ex vivo to in vivo conditions, and that in vivo studies are indispensable to better understand retinal computation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings showing differences between ex vivo and in vivo conditions.

claim: In vivo studies are indispensable to better understand retinal computation.
source: Our results highlight that our knowledge on retinal physiology cannot be simply translated from ex vivo to in vivo conditions, and that in vivo studies are indispensable to better understand retinal computation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: In awake animals, both the baseline and visually evoked firing rates of RGCs were much higher—on average by ~20 Hz—than in those under anesthesia or in an isolated preparation.
source: In awake animals, both the baseline and visually evoked firing rates of RGCs were much higher—on average by ~20 Hz—than in those under anesthesia or in an isolated preparation (Figures 3 and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figures 3 and 6).

claim: High firing activity in awake animals has been widely observed in many brain areas across species.
source: High firing activity in awake animals has been widely observed in many brain areas across species (Greenberg et al., 2008; Sellers et al., 2015; Durand et al., 2016; Wright et al., 2017; De Franceschi and Solomon, 2018; Chen and Song, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: High firing activity could be a general feature of the brain in an awake state, including the retina.
source: Therefore, it could be a general feature of the brain in an awake state, including the retina.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the widespread observation of high firing in awake states across brain areas.

claim: High firing activity leads to a lower DS/OS index value by definition.
source: First, by definition it leads to a lower DS/OS index value calculated as a normalized population vector (Equation 3 in Methods).
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the mathematical definition of the DS/OS index.

claim: The baseline activity level affected the response kinetics.
source: Second, the baseline activity level affected the response kinetics (Figures 4 and 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: The higher the baseline firing is, the higher the conductance of the cell is, hence the shorter the response latency becomes.
source: The higher the baseline firing is, the higher the conductance of the cell is, hence the shorter the response latency becomes (Zohar et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2014; Durand et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Zohar et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2014; Durand et al., 2016).

claim: The dynamic range was altered by baseline activity level.
source: Third, the dynamic range was also altered (Figures 3 and 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figures 3, 6, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).

claim: Many awake ON cells exhibited an OFF-suppressive response, an emerging feature observed only in those cells with high baseline firing rates (~60 Hz).
source: Indeed, many awake ON cells exhibited an OFF-suppressive response, an emerging feature observed only in those cells with high baseline firing rates (~60 Hz).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: OFF-suppressive ON cells likely belong to a known cell type, and altered their response properties due to an increased baseline activity in the awake condition.
source: Instead, these cells likely belong to a known cell type, and altered their response properties due to an increased baseline activity in the awake condition.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the identity of OFF-suppressive ON cells.

claim: One possibility for differences between in vivo and ex vivo retinal responses is the difference in the physiological states of the retina.
source: One possibility is the difference in the physiological states of the retina.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about mechanisms underlying differences.

claim: The retinal pigment epithelium is often removed in an isolated retinal preparation.
source: In particular, the retinal pigment epithelium, a key player for the visual cycle and spatial buffering of ions, is often removed in an isolated retinal preparation.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about ex vivo preparation methods.

claim: A lack of retinal supply can alter the physiological states of the retinal neurons, potentially leading to a change in their visual response properties.
source: A lack of retinal supply can then alter the physiological states of the retinal neurons, potentially leading to a change in their visual response properties.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the effects of ex vivo preparation.

claim: Differences in the input stimulus properties cannot explain the higher firing and faster kinetics observed in awake animals.
source: Therefore, higher baseline activity and faster dynamics observed in awake animals cannot be simply attributed to the difference in the stimulus conditions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the analysis of stimulus conditions and known retinal response properties.

claim: The retina has been assumed to optimize the channel capacity by compressing the visual information as much as possible and conveying signals to the brain using as few spikes as possible.
source: The retina has then been assumed to optimize the channel capacity by compressing the visual information as much as possible and conveying signals to the brain using as few spikes as possible (Attneave, 1954; Barlow and Rosenblith, 1961; Laughlin, 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Attneave, 1954; Barlow and Rosenblith, 1961; Laughlin, 2001).

claim: The efficient coding hypothesis is supported by both ex vivo experimental data and theoretical analyses.
source: This so-called efficient coding hypothesis is supported by both ex vivo experimental data and theoretical analyses.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about the efficient coding hypothesis.

claim: Under ex vivo conditions, many RGCs are silent most of the time and fire spikes at high rates only when their selective stimulus features are presented.
source: Under ex vivo conditions, while some RGCs exhibit high firing under certain conditions (Ke et al., 2014; Smeds et al., 2019), many RGCs are silent most of the time and fire spikes at high rates only when their selective stimulus features are presented (Gollisch and Meister, 2010; Baden et al., 2016; Jouty et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Gollisch and Meister, 2010; Baden et al., 2016; Jouty et al., 2018).

claim: Sparse RGC response helps achieve high efficiency and low redundancy in the visual representation of the retina.
source: This sparse RGC response, ensured by low spontaneous activity and strong nonlinearity (Pitkow and Meister, 2012), helps achieve high efficiency and low redundancy in the visual representation of the retina (Doi et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Pitkow and Meister, 2012; Doi et al., 2012).

claim: Efficient coding principles can explain various physiological properties of the retina, such as separation of retinal outputs into multiple cell types.
source: Furthermore, efficient coding principles can explain various physiological properties of the retina, such as separation of retinal outputs into multiple cell types (Gjorgjieva et al., 2019), even though it cannot fully account for the retinal function (Schwartz, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Gjorgjieva et al., 2019; Schwartz, 2021).

claim: The retinal output characteristics observed in vivo provide a different view on the retinal code than the efficient coding hypothesis.
source: The retinal output characteristics we observed in vivo, however, provide a different view on the retinal code.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings.

claim: RGCs in awake mice generally showed a high baseline activity with more linearized responses.
source: First, unlike ex vivo conditions, RGCs in awake mice generally showed a high baseline activity with more linearized responses (Figures 3 and 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figures 3 and 6).

claim: Many awake ON cells primarily encoded light decrements by suppression from high baseline, rather than light increments by activation from low baseline.
source: Consequently, many awake ON cells primarily encoded light decrements by suppression from high baseline, rather than light increments by activation from low baseline.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Awake ON cells convey the same information as conventional ON cells do but using much more spikes.
source: These cells convey the same information as conventional ON cells do—the more spikes, the higher light intensity—but using much more spikes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data on awake ON cells.

claim: Less variability in the visual response dynamics across different RGC classes was found in vivo.
source: Second, we found less variability in the visual response dynamics across different RGC classes in vivo (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 5E-H).

claim: Temporal coding framework may not be readily applicable in vivo as it requires noticeable differences in spike timing patterns or response latencies between two or more channels.
source: This suggests that temporal coding framework may not be readily applicable in vivo as it requires noticeable differences in spike timing patterns or response latencies between two or more channels, such as ON and OFF pathways converging onto ON–OFF RGCs (Gollisch and Meister, 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and a citation (Gollisch and Meister, 2008).

claim: A linear decoder worked significantly better with the population responses in awake mice.
source: Our modeling analysis indeed demonstrated that awake responses were in favor of a rate code but not a latency-based temporal code (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), and that a linear decoder worked significantly better with the population responses in awake mice (Figure 8), even though an image reconstruction is not necessarily the retina's objective function.
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling analysis based on experimental data (Figure 8).

claim: There is a need to reconsider retinal function in vivo.
source: These results point out a need to reconsider retinal function in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental findings that challenge the efficient coding hypothesis.

claim: One can gain faster response kinetics and wider bandwidths with energy-inefficient retinal coding.
source: As shown in our awake recordings, one can gain faster response kinetics (Figure 5) and wider bandwidths (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental data (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: Redundancy in the dense code helps transmit signals accurately even with intrinsically noisy spike trains.
source: In addition, redundancy in the dense code helps transmit signals accurately even with intrinsically noisy spike trains, as demonstrated by a high performance of a simple linear decoder (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the linear decoding analysis (Figure 8).

claim: The features of dense coding are all highly beneficial from a behavioral viewpoint and thus worth achieving for survival at an expense of energy cost.
source: These features are all highly beneficial from a behavioral viewpoint—for example, to detect predators robustly and promptly—and thus worth achieving for survival at an expense of energy cost.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the behavioral advantages of dense coding.

claim: Dense coding can be a general feature of early sensory processing.
source: Interestingly, dense coding can be a general feature of early sensory processing, as suggested by high baseline firing in vestibular and cochlear nuclei (Fuchs and Kimm, 1975; Rhode and Smith, 1986; Warchol and Dallos, 1990; Beraneck and Cullen, 2007), tonic activity in hair cells (Sachs and Abbas, 1974; Wu et al., 2016), and dark current in vertebrate photoreceptors (Hagins et al., 1970; Okawa et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research on other sensory systems.

claim: The energy cost of dense retinal coding may not be so problematic with a relatively small number of neurons.
source: In fact, the energy cost of dense retinal coding may not be so problematic with a relatively small number of neurons, as opposed to the total energy required for operating ~109 neurons in the cortex where sparse coding has certain advantages from the viewpoints of both energy efficiency and sensory processing (Olshausen and Field, 1996; Asari et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation and supported by citations (Olshausen and Field, 1996; Asari et al., 2006).

claim: The retina may employ different coding principles under different light levels.
source: The retina, however, may employ different coding principles under different light levels (Wang et al., 2011; Tikidji-Hamburyan et al., 2015; Borghuis et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Wang et al., 2011; Tikidji-Hamburyan et al., 2015; Borghuis et al., 2018).

claim: All in vivo recordings were done in a high-mesopic/low-photopic range (at ~103 R*/photoreceptor/s).
source: All our in vivo recordings were done in a high-mesopic/low-photopic range (at ~103 R*/photoreceptor/s; see Methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: In a scotopic condition, ex vivo studies have reported a high tonic firing rate for OFF RGC types (~50 Hz, OFF sustained alpha cells in mice; ~20 Hz, OFF parasol cells in primates), while a low tonic firing for corresponding ON cell types (<1 Hz).
source: In a scotopic condition, in contrast, ex vivo studies have reported a high tonic firing rate for OFF RGC types (~50 Hz, OFF sustained alpha cells in mice; Smeds et al., 2019; ~20 Hz, OFF parasol cells in primates; Ala-Laurila and Rieke, 2014), while a low tonic firing for corresponding ON cell types (<1 Hz).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Smeds et al., 2019; Ala-Laurila and Rieke, 2014).

claim: In scotopic conditions, ON cells were shown to be responsible for light detection by firing in the silent background.
source: Since these ON cells were shown to be responsible for light detection by firing in the silent background (Smeds et al., 2019), here the retina seems to operate with a sparse feature detection strategy.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Smeds et al., 2019).

claim: In scotopic conditions, the retina seems to operate with a sparse feature detection strategy.
source: Since these ON cells were shown to be responsible for light detection by firing in the silent background (Smeds et al., 2019), here the retina seems to operate with a sparse feature detection strategy.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cited research on scotopic vision.

claim: Anesthetics generally lower the excitability of nerve cells.
source: Anesthetics generally lower the excitability of nerve cells: for example, isoflurane acts on the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) type A receptors to silence the brain (Jenkins et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Jenkins et al., 1999).

claim: It makes sense that the retinal outputs were reduced under anesthesia and showed slower dynamics than in awake animals.
source: It thus makes sense that the retinal outputs were reduced under anesthesia (Figures 3 and 6) and showed slower dynamics (Figures 4 and 5) than in awake animals.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the known effects of anesthetics and experimental data (Figures 3-6).

claim: It is difficult to generalize the effects of anesthesia because multiple mechanisms of action are involved, exerting complex effects on the sensory systems in anesthetic- and dose-dependent manners.
source: It is, however, difficult to generalize the effects of anesthesia because multiple mechanisms of action are involved, exerting complex effects on the sensory systems in anesthetic- and dose-dependent manners (Populin, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Populin, 2005).

claim: Visual cortical responses are reduced under anesthesia.
source: For example, while visual cortical responses are reduced under anesthesia (Haider et al., 2013; Vaiceliunaite et al., 2013), auditory responses are enhanced (Raz et al., 2014; Sellers et al., 2015) and the response latency becomes shorter in the auditory pathway (Ter-Mikaelian et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Haider et al., 2013; Vaiceliunaite et al., 2013).

claim: Auditory responses are enhanced under anesthesia.
source: For example, while visual cortical responses are reduced under anesthesia (Haider et al., 2013; Vaiceliunaite et al., 2013), auditory responses are enhanced (Raz et al., 2014; Sellers et al., 2015) and the response latency becomes shorter in the auditory pathway (Ter-Mikaelian et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Raz et al., 2014; Sellers et al., 2015).

claim: The response latency becomes shorter in the auditory pathway under anesthesia.
source: For example, while visual cortical responses are reduced under anesthesia (Haider et al., 2013; Vaiceliunaite et al., 2013), auditory responses are enhanced (Raz et al., 2014; Sellers et al., 2015) and the response latency becomes shorter in the auditory pathway (Ter-Mikaelian et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Ter-Mikaelian et al., 2007).

claim: The study's results are consistent with previous studies on the effects of anesthesia in the early visual system.
source: Our results are nevertheless consistent with previous studies on the effects of anesthesia in the early visual system.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from comparison with previous studies.

claim: Anesthesia reduces the overall activity of both SC and dLGN neurons, and leads to multiple changes in temporal processing such as reduced sensitivity to high temporal frequencies and longer response latencies.
source: Specifically, anesthesia reduces the overall activity of both SC and dLGN neurons, and leads to multiple changes in temporal processing of these two major retinorecipient areas, such as reduced sensitivity to high temporal frequencies and longer response latencies (Zhao et al., 2014; Durand et al., 2016; De Franceschi and Solomon, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Zhao et al., 2014; Durand et al., 2016; De Franceschi and Solomon, 2018).

claim: The consistent findings suggest that changes in the response dynamics arise largely from the retina.
source: While different anesthetics were used in these studies (urethane as opposed to isoflurane and FMM), our consistent findings suggest that such changes in the response dynamics arise largely from the retina.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the consistency of findings across studies.

claim: The effects of anesthesia on spatial response properties seem more complex than on temporal properties.
source: In contrast, the effects of anesthesia on spatial response properties seem more complex.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature on anesthesia effects.

claim: Spatial processing remains largely intact in dLGN under anesthesia.
source: While spatial processing remains largely intact in dLGN (Durand et al., 2016), lower sensitivity to contrast and larger receptive field sizes were reported in SC under urethane anesthesia (De Franceschi and Solomon, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Durand et al., 2016).

claim: Lower sensitivity to contrast and larger receptive field sizes were reported in SC under urethane anesthesia.
source: While spatial processing remains largely intact in dLGN (Durand et al., 2016), lower sensitivity to contrast and larger receptive field sizes were reported in SC under urethane anesthesia (De Franceschi and Solomon, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (De Franceschi and Solomon, 2018).

claim: SC neurons show increased orientation selectivity under isoflurane anesthesia.
source: Moreover, SC neurons show increased orientation selectivity (OS) under isoflurane anesthesia (Kasai and Isa, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Kasai and Isa, 2022).

claim: A larger fraction of DS/OS cells was found under both isoflurane and FMM anesthesia than in the awake condition.
source: Here we also found a larger fraction of DS/OS cells under both isoflurane and FMM anesthesia than in the awake condition (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from the study (Figure 2D-F).

claim: The larger fraction of DS/OS cells under anesthesia could be due to the difference in the baseline firing rate.
source: This, however, could be due to the difference in the baseline firing rate (Figure 3) as the DS/OS index is defined by a normalized population vector in response to moving gratings (Equation 3 in Methods; Mazurek et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the definition of DS/OS index and experimental data (Figure 3).
